messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marlene is a 71-year-old forensic analyst, married, who was referred for psychological assessment following a physical assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. She was attacked in a parking structure adjacent to her office building late one evening — a man grabbed her from behind, pinned her arms, and struck her repeatedly about the face and upper body before fleeing. She was left on the concrete floor, her hands visible beneath a flickering fluorescent light, blood on her fingers, the smell of exhaust and cold cement surrounding her. It is the image of her own hands — splayed and trembling on that floor — that has lodged most persistently in her mind, and it is why, now, the sight of her own hands at certain angles, or the hands of a colleague reaching across a laboratory bench, can send a jolt of alarm through her body that feels entirely indistinguishable from that night.

In the weeks that followed the assault, Marlene attempted to return to her work in forensic analysis — a field that had always given her a sense of competence and purpose. But the laboratory environment, where she routinely examines physical evidence and handles detailed photographic material, became unexpectedly hostile terrain. When a memory of the assault intruded — often triggered by the sight of specific body parts in forensic photographs, or by a colleague asking her casually about a case timeline — the memory did not arrive as a coherent narrative. It came in fragments: a flash of rage so intense it frightened her, or, in other moments, a strange blankness, as though she were reviewing footage of someone else's life. She found herself pushing the memory away before it could fully form, telling herself she was simply being efficient, staying focused. She had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that if she allowed herself to think about it fully, something in her would give way entirely.

That belief — that she was inadequate to the task of her own memory — began to colour everything. She stopped exercising, something she had done consistently for decades, because physical exertion brought her heart rate up in a way that felt dangerous, too close to the panic of that night. She began restricting her food, not consciously at first, but as a way of maintaining a sense of control over a body that now felt unreliable. She rearranged her seating in every room she entered — at work, at restaurants, at family dinners — so that her back was always against a wall and she could see the full space in front of her. These habits felt rational, even necessary. But each one quietly confirmed what she had already begun to suspect about herself: that she was not the person she used to be, that the happiness she had once taken for granted was simply gone, replaced by a misery she could not name to her husband without feeling she was burdening him with something he could not fix.

The strategies that were meant to contain her distress began, over months, to amplify it. By avoiding physical activity and restricting her eating, Marlene kept her body in a state of low-grade depletion that made emotional regulation harder, and the memories, when they broke through, felt more overwhelming rather than less. The avoidance of full recall meant the memory never resolved — it remained jagged, ready to be snagged by any passing stimulus. Sitting with her back to the wall, scanning every room, meant she was always, in some part of her nervous system, still in that parking structure. These vigilant postures kept the triggers close, so that conversations about the future — what she and her husband might do when she retired, where they might travel — produced a sudden, almost physical resistance, as though the future were a country she no longer had clearance to enter.

What finally brought Marlene to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. A junior colleague asked her, gently, to walk him through an old case she had handled. She felt rage rise in her chest before a single word left her mouth — rage she could not explain and could not contain — and she left the room without speaking. She sat in her car for forty minutes. She told her husband that evening, for the first time, that she was not managing. What she is most afraid of, she said quietly, is that she has already become someone she does not recognise. What she is hoping for, with considerably less certainty, is that she might not be right about that.
